newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - KEXIM seen facing difficult mk.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - KEXIM seen facing difficult mk.

text.p: Export-Import Bank of Korea launched its US$500 million global bond into a difficult market on Tuesday.
KEXIM's five-year bond will be priced during New York hours to yield 44-46 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. Morgan Stanley and Salomon Brothers are lead managers.
"The deal has been met by a slow reception because people are obviously concerned about what is going on in Korea," said a syndicate manager at a European bank in Hong Kong.
Korean financial markets have been hit hard by news emerging late last month of a major default on debt payments by Korean conglomerate Hanbo's flagship Hanbo Steel.
Banks with large exposures to Hanbo have suffered the most, but the commercial banks in general have seen their debt issues fare poorly in the secondary market.
Thus far, highly rated quasi-sovereigns such as KEXIM have escaped that fate. For example, KEXIM has no relation with Hanbo, Salomon Brothers has pointed out.
But bankers said that investors increasingly are taking a wait-and-see approach to Korean credits on fears the entire financial sector may be in trouble.
"The fears aren't about KEXIM itself, which is a great credit, but in general about Korea," said a trader.
Korea Electric Power Corp's recent Yankee bond has widened considerably in the secondary market, traders reported.
The US$300 million 10-year bond was priced to yield 45 basis points last week but that spread has since widened by up to 10 basis points, they said.
Some bankers complained that the Kepco deal was priced too tightly from the start.
Bankers said the troubles in Korea could have wider implications for Asian debt markets if Korean banks find that their funding costs continue to rise.
These banks have become major lenders to other Asian borrrowers over the past year, particularly to those offering high yields.
On Tuesday, sources in Tokyo told Reuters that Japanese branches of Korean banks are paying a premium of about 10 basis points over the prevailing unsecured overnight call rate of about 0.50 percent.
In other news, details emerged on a US$200 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue for Malaysia's DCB Bank.
Merrill Lynch International, J.P. Morgan Securities and Sakura Finance Asia are the leads.
